# Reinforcement Foundations

## 1. What Reinforcement Means
Don’t Shoot the Dog! is about how to train and teach almost anyone through reinforcement. Reinforcement is not simply a system of rewards and punishments. A reinforcer is an event that occurs during a behavior or upon its completion and increases the likelihood that the behavior will occur again in the future. The behavior and the reinforcement have to be connected in real time. When that connection works, the behavior becomes more frequent.

A consequence can involve something the learner likes and wants more of, or it can involve escaping or avoiding something unpleasant. The key is the result: if the behavior becomes more likely in the future, the consequence functioned as reinforcement. If the behavior does not increase, either the reinforcement was too early or too late, or what was selected was not actually reinforcing to that individual. Reinforcement training therefore depends on observation, quick thinking and continuous adjustment to the learner.

## 2. Real-Time Reinforcement and the Learner’s Perspective
Reinforcement has to occur in the instant. The learner needs to know that what they are doing right now is what earned the prize. Yelling is usually less useful than watching for behavior you like and reinforcing it when it happens; this can also keep the peace instead of creating constant conflict.

A reinforcer is anything that occurs in conjunction with an action and increases the probability that the action will occur again. Positive reinforcement involves something the subject wants. Negative reinforcement strengthens behavior because changing the behavior allows the subject to avoid or end something aversive. A behavior must already be occurring in some form before it can be reinforced. Find a small version of the desired behavior first, then strengthen it.

Positive reinforcement can also be used on yourself. Instead of focusing only on what you did wrong, notice and praise successful behavior. Reinforcers are relative, not absolute: the same event can affect different individuals differently. Rain may be welcome to a duck and unwelcome to a cat. What matters is the learner’s actual response, not the trainer’s assumption about what should be rewarding.

## 3. Negative Reinforcement and Punishment
Negative reinforcement increases behavior, but it does not require something the learner wants. Behavior can be strengthened by an aversive stimulus when a change in behavior makes that aversive stimulus stop. A yell, a hit, a contemptuous glance or even a disapproving sniff can function in this way if the learner can halt or avoid it by changing behavior. The pattern is: an aversive condition is present, a new behavior occurs, the aversive condition stops, and the new behavior is strengthened.

This is different from punishment. Punishment follows behavior and may involve the loss of something desirable or another unwanted consequence. Deliberate punishment is often delivered too late to communicate clearly what should change. Reinforcers strengthen behavior in a predictable direction; punishment does not reliably tell the learner what to do instead and can produce unpredictable future changes.

Reinforcement is a process defined by its result. Each case of negative reinforcement depends on an aversive condition that can be escaped or avoided. Overusing negative reinforcement can also produce the undesirable side effects associated with punishment. A variety of reinforcers is useful, and effective training requires taking an interest in what the individual actually wants or responds to.

## 4. Reinforcement Is Information
The consequence is not only a payoff; it is information. It tells the learner which action mattered. This is why precision, timing and the learner’s perspective are central. A consequence that the trainer intends as reinforcement but that does not increase behavior is not functioning as reinforcement. The trainer must judge the process by the learner’s future behavior, not by the trainer’s intention.

# Timing, Signals and Communication

## 5. Timing and Size of Reinforcement
The timing of the arrival of a reinforcer is information. It tells the learner exactly what the trainer likes. A delayed reinforcer can have a harmful effect because it may become attached to the wrong behavior. We often trust words to compensate for bad timing, but verbal explanation cannot fully repair a poorly timed consequence.

An early reinforcer is also ineffective. Trying to reinforce a behavior before it has occurred becomes bribery rather than precise reinforcement. With negative reinforcement, if the aversive condition does not stop the instant the desired result is achieved, it is neither useful reinforcement nor useful information; it becomes noise. Work can feel peculiarly unsatisfying for the same reason when the reinforcers, however good, always arrive too late.

How large should a reinforcer be? Often, as small as you can get away with. The difficulty of the task affects the appropriate size. A jackpot is a reward much larger than the normal reinforcer that arrives as a surprise.

## 6. Conditioned Reinforcers, the Click and Keep-Going Signals
Often the real reinforcement cannot be delivered at the exact instant the learner performs the behavior. A conditioned reinforcer solves this timing problem. It begins as a meaningless signal — a sound, light, word, motion or other stimulus — and gains meaning by being deliberately paired with a real reinforcer. Everyday life is full of conditioned signals: phone rings, message notifications, whistles, ringtones, holiday cues and even the smell of a dentist’s office can acquire positive or negative meaning because of what they predict.

Positive-reinforcement training should establish a conditioned reinforcer by pairing the signal with the real reinforcer. A phrase such as “Good job” can become meaningful when it reliably predicts something the learner values. But conditioned reinforcers must be protected. If they are thrown around meaninglessly, their force is diluted. False or automatic praise soon loses information value.

A click is a precise conditioned reinforcer. It ends the behavior and identifies exactly what behavior is being reinforced. It gives the learner clear control over the problem: after a while, the learner does not merely repeat behavior but actively offers and varies behavior. This is part of operant conditioning and shaping. The rule is one click, one treat. Repeated clicks without reinforcement can eventually extinguish the click’s significance.

A keep-going signal serves a different purpose. It can be inserted before the terminating click to communicate that the learner is moving in the right direction and should continue. It does not have to be paired directly with a primary reinforcer every time; if it reliably comes before the final click and reinforcement, the learner learns that it predicts progress toward eventual reinforcement. The specific stimulus can be a clicker, word, shout, wave or another clear cue. What matters is that it is well established and used precisely.

## 7. Conditioned Aversive Signals and No-Reward Markers
A conditioned aversive signal communicates that what the learner is doing now is not acceptable and that something unpleasant may happen unless the behavior changes. A simple “No” can be established as a conditioned negative reinforcer: the signal gives the learner a chance to stop or change the behavior and thereby avoid the aversive consequence. For example, a warning can come before a leash correction; if behavior changes, the correction is avoided.

Punishing without warning turns the event into simple punishment with no reliable information about what future behavior should replace the old one. It can also accumulate unwanted side effects. Failing to use a conditioned warning in correction-based training increases the number of actual aversive events and can slow learning, sometimes requiring many repetitions before the learner sorts out what is expected.

A no-reward marker is different again. When a learner is actively trying different behaviors to discover what works, a signal can communicate that a particular attempt will not be reinforced. It means, in effect, “not that one — try something else.” This is useful only after the learner understands the reinforcement game and is willing to vary behavior in search of a response that earns the click.

# Schedules, Accidental Learning and Self-Reinforcement

## 8. Schedules of Reinforcement
Constant reinforcement is most important during the learning stage. A beginner needs many reinforcers so the connection is clear. Once a behavior is learned, reinforcement can become occasional and unpredictable through a variable schedule. A behavior maintained on a variable schedule can become extremely persistent because the learner does not know when the next payoff will come.

The starting-car example illustrates this. If a car never starts, eventually you stop trying. If it sometimes starts immediately and sometimes only after 15 or 30 minutes, you may keep trying because success remains possible but unpredictable. Gambling uses the same principle: uncertainty about when the jackpot will arrive powerfully maintains behavior. From a manipulator’s point of view, this can become the disturbing principle that someone can be kept performing as long as they receive what they want once in a while.

Variable reinforcement can work against you when you are trying to eliminate behavior. One cigarette, one drink or one occasional payoff can revive and strengthen a pattern that was beginning to disappear.

There are exceptions. When behavior involves solving a puzzle, test or problem, reinforcement communicates whether a choice was correct, so unpredictable reinforcement can interfere with learning the solution. Long-duration behavior can instead use fixed schedules based on a predetermined amount of work, behavior or time: a fish every six jumps, a game after a month of hard training, or payday on Friday. Both fixed and variable schedules can maintain very long behavior sequences.

Delayed gratification only works if the eventual reward remains strong enough to justify the effort. When a person consistently expends more energy than the benefits they receive, a task or job can reach the point where it no longer feels worth doing. Long tasks also create a starting problem: there are endless reasons not to begin now. A useful strategy is to reinforce the act of getting started rather than waiting for the entire task to be completed.

## 9. Superstitious Behavior and Group Reinforcement
Superstitious behavior develops through accidental reinforcement when a behavior is unrelated to the outcome but is followed by success often enough that the learner treats it as necessary. Someone might chew a pencil during a test, succeed, and begin to believe the chewing helped produce the success. The practical lesson is to separate methods that genuinely affect outcomes from methods that merely coexist with reinforcement. We should also look for superstitious behavior in ourselves.

Reinforcement can also be social and organized through group recognition. A crowd can encourage a shy person and immediately reward a bold one. But the same mechanism creates a danger: when everybody agrees and roars approval, social reinforcement can become stronger than concern for what is actually true or right.

Good training insights do not always lend themselves easily to verbal explanation. Observation, timing and practical feel can sometimes precede a perfect verbal theory.

## 10. Reinforcing Yourself
A certain amount of reinforcement is desirable simply for surviving ordinary life. Healthy reinforcers can include walking with friends, talking with friends, reading a book and other activities that replenish energy and make effort sustainable. Unhealthy immediate reinforcers can include alcohol, smoking, drugs and other behaviors that feel rewarding now while carrying harmful long-term consequences. The question is not only whether something reinforces behavior in the moment, but what kind of behavior and life that reinforcer is helping to maintain.

# Shaping — Developing Performance Without Strain or Pain

## 11. What Shaping Is
Shaping means taking a very small tendency in the right direction and moving it one small step at a time toward the ultimate goal. Success is not just a matter of persistence, time, repetitions or drilling. Using the laws that govern shaping makes work more efficient and can produce steady progress without unnecessary strain or pain. Done well, shaping can move extremely fast.

## 12. Methods Versus Principles
Shaping has two aspects. Methods are the behaviors to be developed and the sequence of steps used to develop them. Principles concern how, when and why those behaviors are reinforced. Methods matter for learning a skill, but successful application of reinforcement principles can be the difference between an adequate teacher and a great one. Good principles make shaping faster, happier and more successful.

## 13. Law 1 — Raise the Criterion in Small Enough Steps
The learner must retain a realistic chance of earning reinforcement. Raise the criterion within a range the learner can approach. Raising the criterion changes the rules for earning reinforcement, so the learner needs an opportunity to discover the new rule. If the increase is too large, behavior can break down. Raise criteria at whatever interval makes steady improvement easy; small enough steps are often the fastest path.

## 14. Law 2 — Train One Aspect at a Time
Different behaviors can be trained in the same general period, but within a particular behavior work on one criterion at a time. Vary tasks as needed, moving on after progress, but do not ask one reinforcer to communicate two separate pieces of information. If speed, accuracy, posture and power are all being changed at once, the learner may not know what earned reinforcement.

## 15. Law 3 — Put the Current Response on a Variable Schedule Before Raising the Criterion
Once a level of behavior is established, reinforce it variably before demanding a better response. When an expected reinforcer is occasionally skipped, the next response is likely to vary. That variation gives the trainer a chance to select a stronger or better response. With an inexperienced learner, begin with small variation so the learner experiences occasional non-reinforcement without abandoning the behavior.

## 16. Law 4 — Relax Old Criteria When Introducing a New One
When a new aspect of a skill is introduced, temporarily relax older criteria. Previously learned behavior is not necessarily forgotten, but the pressure of assimilating a new requirement can temporarily make older parts fall apart. These mistakes often clear by themselves. Reprimands, shouting and repeated attention to temporary errors can make them more persistent.

## 17. Law 5 — Stay Ahead of the Learner
Plan the shaping program so that if the learner makes a sudden leap forward, you already know what to reinforce next. Breakthroughs are golden opportunities for rapid progress. If the plan is to move from A to B and the learner suddenly performs B perfectly after only a couple of reinforcements, have C and D ready so the breakthrough does not run out of useful reinforcement.

## 18. Law 6 — Don’t Change Trainers in Midstream
Changing trainers during a half-learned behavior risks major slowdown because timing, signals and gradually escalating criteria can become inconsistent. Keeping a behavior in one trainer’s hands usually preserves continuity. Change trainers when training is going nowhere; if little or no learning is occurring, there is less to lose by switching.

## 19. Law 7 — If One Shaping Procedure Does Not Work, Try Another
There are many ways to shape the same behavior. If one method is not eliciting progress, use another. If a child is bored by or afraid of one method, switch. The same shaping method does not work equally well for every individual. The goal is learning, not loyalty to a procedure.

## 20. Law 8 — Don’t Interrupt Training Carelessly
Removing attention in the middle of training can function as punishment. During skill training, the trainer should remain attentive to the learner or class until the period is over. Distraction can cause the trainer to miss a golden opportunity to reinforce, or it can accidentally punish good behavior that happened just as attention disappeared. Withdrawal of attention is powerful and should be used deliberately, not carelessly or unfairly.

## 21. Law 9 — If a Learned Behavior Deteriorates, Review the Shaping
A well-learned behavior can become rusty, temporarily disappear under unusual circumstances, or be disrupted by punishment and other aversive events that interfere with unrelated behavior. Sometimes the cause is never identified. The fastest repair is often to recreate the original shaping path very rapidly, reinforcing once or twice at each old level under the new circumstances. This review can work for both physical and mental skills.

## 22. Law 10 — Quit While You Are Ahead
When training stops is less important than what is happening when it stops. Whenever possible, finish after a successful response rather than after frustration or deterioration. The last behavior accomplished is likely to be remembered strongly. End on success.

## 23. The Central Shaping Pattern
Effective shaping does not depend on forcing performance through endless repetition. The pattern is: small achievable steps, precise reinforcement, gradually increasing criteria and steady progress. When the trainer understands these principles, complex behavior can be developed smoothly, positively and sometimes extraordinarily quickly.
